settlement-survey-s1.title: Three ways of dividing farmland, seen from above

settlement-survey-s2.title: The Land Ordinance of 1785, in summary
settlement-survey-s2.html: In 1785 the US Congress (then under the Articles of Confederation) passed the Land Ordinance. In our summary: public land in the West, starting northwest of the Ohio River, was to be surveyed before it was sold. Surveyors drew east-west and north-south lines to divide it into townships, squares 6 miles on each side. Each township was split into 36 sections of 1 square mile (640 acres). One section in each township was set aside to support a public school. Land was then sold by the section or in parts of sections.

agricultural-origins-s1.title: Some early hearths of agriculture

agricultural-origins-s2.title: The potato in Ireland
agricultural-origins-s2.html: LevlPrep summary, 2026, based on historians' accounts. The potato was domesticated in the Andes of South America. Spanish ships carried it to Europe in the late 1500s, and it reached Ireland soon after. The potato grew well in Ireland's cool, wet climate and fed a family on a small plot. By the 1840s, millions of poor rural families in Ireland depended on one kind of potato for most of their food. From 1845, a plant disease called blight destroyed the crop several years in a row. In the famine that followed, about 1 million people died and more than 1 million left Ireland, many for the United States.

second-agricultural-revolution-s2.title: A new machine for the harvest, 1831
second-agricultural-revolution-s2.html: LevlPrep summary, 2026, based on US farm histories. In 1831, Cyrus McCormick showed a horse-drawn reaper in Virginia. Before it, workers cut wheat by hand with a scythe or cradle, and a crew could harvest only a few acres a day. Pulled by horses, the reaper cut grain as it moved, so a few people could harvest many times more land in a day. By the 1850s, reapers were being sold across the wheat lands of the US Midwest.

agriculture-consequences-s2.title: The Aral Sea
agriculture-consequences-s2.html: LevlPrep summary, 2026, of reports by the UN Environment Programme and NASA. The Aral Sea, between Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, was once one of the four largest lakes in the world. From the 1960s, Soviet planners diverted the two rivers that fed it to irrigate cotton fields in the desert. The sea shrank to a small fraction of its size and split into parts. Fishing towns were left far from the water. Winds now lift salty dust from the dry seabed onto farmland, and many irrigated fields became salty. In 2005, Kazakhstan finished a dam that helped the small northern part of the sea rise again.

women-in-agriculture-s1.html: Source: FAO, The Status of Women in Agrifood Systems, 2023.

women-in-agriculture-s2.title: Gaps between women and men in farming
women-in-agriculture-s2.html: From FAO, The Status of Women in Agrifood Systems (2023), in our summary. Women in farm wage work earn about 82 cents for every dollar men earn. On farms of the same size, farms run by women produce about 24% less, a gap FAO links to unequal access to land, credit, seeds, fertilizer, training and markets. In 40 of the 46 countries that reported, men were more likely than women to own or have secure rights to farmland. FAO estimates that closing the gaps in farm productivity and wages could reduce the number of people facing food insecurity by about 45 million.
